# Social Chain of Thought: A Multi-Agent Architecture Grounded in Medical Differential Diagnosis Methodology

- **Authors**: Del Coburn, Scott Sanner, Dan Silver
- **Venue**: cs.AI
- **Published**: 2026-08-11
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11420>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.11420v1>
- **Topics**: reasoning-training, test-time-scaling
- **Relevance score**: reasoning-training 0.50, test-time-scaling 0.57

## In one line

Structures multi-agent medical differential diagnosis as rounds of persona-conditioned specialist deliberation, and shows the recall advantage is not reproduced by best-of-n sampling from the same model, concentrates entirely in the cases where monolithic inference fails, and reverses on the easiest quartile.

## Problem

Multi-agent approaches to medical diagnosis have been proposed without establishing when they are needed, why they help, or where they beat monolithic inference -- and the question matters because more than 5 percent of ChatGPT messages globally are healthcare-related. The specific obstacle is endogeneity: a single model evaluating its own output propagates the correlation bias inherent in the source of generation, so self-evaluation cannot be fixed by scaling the model or letting it think longer. It has to be approached with intentional heterogeneity, which is what a multi-agent architecture can supply and repeated sampling cannot.

## Contributions

- A multi-round deliberative architecture for differential diagnosis in which heterogeneity is produced by persona conditioning and measured as error decorrelation, rather than assumed from having several agents.
- A control that most multi-agent work omits: best-of-n repeated sampling at up to 35 samples, with and without a judge, from the same model -- none of which reproduces the recall advantage, which is what licenses attributing the gain to structured heterogeneity rather than to extra passes.
- A difficulty-conditioned result reported in both directions: 15.1 F1 points on the hardest quartile against an 8.3-point precision loss on the easiest, so the method is shown to have a regime rather than a uniform benefit.
- A convergence-pathway analysis tracing where each correct diagnosis entered, showing that the share arriving through late refinement rises from 7 percent on easy cases to 36 percent where the baseline recovered nothing -- direct evidence that agents revising in response to one another is the operative mechanism.
- An empirically located viability threshold, with the sub-threshold failure mode analysed rather than excluded: a 1.5B model recovers 70 terms its baseline missed while destroying 122 the baseline had, because it cannot push back on weak proposals from other agents.

## Method

Social Chain of Thought runs a multi-round pipeline modelled on how specialists actually deliberate over a differential diagnosis, with heterogeneity produced by persona conditioning rather than by different model backends -- the authors state plainly that with a shared backend endogeneity remains an issue, and argue the gain is that the reasoning becomes more transparent as well as more varied. Specialists propose diagnoses with supporting evidence, see each other's proposals over successive rounds, and revise; a refinement round produces consensus. The comparison set is deliberately hostile to the paper's own thesis: single-agent baselines, one-agent versions of the same pipeline (which isolate the structure from the multiplicity), and best-of-n repeated sampling at n up to 35 both with and without a judge, so that any gain has to survive matched-compute repeated sampling from the same model. Evaluation is on 570 open differential-diagnosis vignettes scored by macro recall, precision and F1 over ground-truth diagnosis terms, with cases stratified into quartiles by how well the monolithic baseline did on them, and a separate subset where the baseline recovered nothing at all. Error decorrelation across specialists is measured directly under temperature and persona conditioning, separately and jointly, and the convergence pathway of each true-positive diagnosis is tracked -- whether it entered early, shifted mid-way, or arrived only in late refinement.

## Results

Repeated sampling does not reproduce the effect: best-of-5, best-of-35 and best-of-35 with a judge all fall short of the five-agent pipeline on recall, which is the paper's central control and the reason the gain is attributed to heterogeneity rather than to additional passes. The benefit is sharply conditioned on difficulty and the authors report both directions. On the hardest quartile, F1 rises 15.1 points from 0.212 to 0.363, a relative lift of 71.4 percent; on the easiest quartile precision falls 8.3 points, so the lift flips sign by the top quartile. The convergence analysis supplies the mechanism rather than asserting it: the share of true-positive diagnoses arriving only through late refinement grows monotonically with difficulty -- 7 percent in the easiest quartile, 19 in the hardest, and 36 percent on the subset where the baseline recovered zero -- so the cases that depend on agents revising in response to each other are exactly the cases monolithic inference fails. Across the full set, 11 percent of the 703 recovered ground-truth terms enter during refinement, rising to 35 percent among the 89 baseline-failure cases, where at least one ground-truth term is recovered in 48 of 89. The most useful negative result is a viability threshold, investigated rather than reported as noise. A 1.5B model appeared to mark the lower bound because its aggregate performance degraded, and the breakdown shows why: it recovers 70 ground-truth terms in cases where its own baseline fails completely, but fails entirely in 159 cases where the baseline recovered 122 terms, so it creates more failures than it resolves. The authors attribute this to lacking the knowledge to push back on weak proposals from other agents, making heterogeneity destabilising rather than productive, and name 1.5 billion parameters as the empirical floor for social inference in this domain.

## Limitations

Stated: the demonstration is not exhaustive and other configurations remain untested; the comparison with frontier models is described as exploratory and restricted by proprietary API cost; more open-weight testing is wanted; and the authors flag that persona conditioning risks reproducing stereotypes the models were trained on. They are also explicit that a shared model backend leaves the endogeneity problem the architecture is meant to address only partly addressed, since the personas are simulated rather than genuinely independent. Not stated but worth noticing: difficulty quartiles are defined by the baseline's own F1 on each case, so the hardest quartile is selected for baseline failure and some of the 71.4 percent relative lift is regression toward the mean -- the convergence-pathway analysis is what makes the mechanistic reading credible, not the quartile lift itself. The headline is a recall advantage while the easiest-quartile cost is a precision loss, and in a diagnostic setting those have very different consequences; no operating-point analysis or downstream harm framing is offered. Evaluation is against ground-truth diagnosis term lists on 570 vignettes with no clinician assessment of the differentials produced.

## Why it matters here

- **reasoning-training**: Read as a training-and-architecture result rather than a medical one, the useful part is the viability threshold and how it was found. Aggregate performance for a 1.5B model degraded under the same pipeline that helps a 32B one, and instead of dropping the model the authors decomposed the outcome: it recovers 70 ground-truth terms in cases where its own baseline fails completely, and destroys 122 in cases where the baseline succeeded, failing entirely in 159 of them. The diagnosis they give is that the model lacks the knowledge to push back on weak proposals from other agents, so heterogeneity becomes destabilising rather than productive. That reframes multi-agent deliberation as something with a capability prerequisite -- a model has to be able to disagree competently before disagreement is worth arranging -- and it is measurable in advance from the net of recovered against destroyed items rather than from an aggregate score, which shows only that it did not work. The paper also states an argument the archive should keep for evaluating any self-verification scheme: a single model evaluating its own output propagates the correlation bias of the source that generated it, so endogeneity is not addressed by scaling or by longer thinking, and the authors concede their own persona-based heterogeneity only partly addresses it because the backend is shared. Their error-decorrelation measurements under persona and temperature conditioning are the right way to check that claim rather than assert it.
- **test-time-scaling**: This is one of the better-controlled comparisons in the archive between spending inference budget on more samples and spending it on differently-conditioned agents. The control is the point: best-of-5, best-of-35, and best-of-35 with a judge all fail to match the five-agent pipeline's recall, so the effect is not more passes. That places it alongside the archive's other evidence that what varies matters more than how much -- input paraphrase diversity beating output diversity at matched compute, and a reranker over a shortlist beating query-time rationale generation. Two findings sharpen how the archive should read multi-agent scaling claims generally. First, the benefit is regime-dependent and the paper measures the reversal rather than averaging over it: 15.1 F1 points on the hardest quartile against an 8.3-point precision loss on the easiest, which is the same shape as the archive's other results where added inference structure amplifies whatever the base system was already doing. Second, the convergence-pathway analysis is a mechanism check most aggregation work lacks -- tracking whether each correct answer entered early, shifted, or arrived only in late refinement, and finding the late-refinement share rising from 7 percent on easy cases to 36 percent where the baseline recovered nothing. That distinguishes 'the ensemble surfaced an answer one member already had' from 'the answer emerged from members revising against each other', which a majority-vote number cannot. The caution to carry: difficulty quartiles are defined by the baseline's own performance, so the headline relative lift is partly regression to the mean, and the convergence analysis rather than the quartile number is what carries the argument.

## Abstract

Medical diagnostic reasoning is a high-impact use case for LLMs that carries significant implications for the health and wellbeing of users. When OpenAI (2026) reports that more than 5% of ChatGPT messages globally are healthcare-related, the transparency of these systems becomes a serious design concern. This is especially true for complex cases, where differential diagnosis often requires integrating multiple forms of specialist reasoning. Existing work has proposed multi-agent approaches to medical diagnosis, but it remains unclear when such systems are needed, why they help, and where they outperform monolithic inference. We introduce Social Chain of Thought (SCoT),a multi-round pipeline for medical differential diagnosis that structures multi-agent interaction as a deliberative framework for collabora. tive LLM reasoning. Evaluating SCoT against single-agent baselines, one-agent pipeline ablations, and best-of-n scaling, we show that its recall advantage is not reproduced by monolithic inference alone. SCoT is most successful in the hardest diagnostic cases, where multiple rounds of specialist conversation help recover ground-truth diagnoses and converge on a higher-recall differential.
